rows.description: A ten-year-old hears relatives praising her brother's marks and starts to feel she is the less loved one. Comparison, even unintended, turns siblings into competitors for the same limited approval.
Each child counts who got the bigger share, the later bedtime or the new phone, and demands exact equality. Underneath is not the object but a need to know they matter as much.
Mocking a sibling's failure, or running to tell on him, becomes a way to gain adult favour. Both lose, since the parent is tired and the sibling now has a real grievance.

rows.subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]
rows.description: The younger sibling feels bossed and left out of the older ones' games, and complains of unfairness. She wants to be looked up to and taken seriously, not merely tolerated.

The parent praises each child for their own effort and strengths and lets them solve small quarrels themselves, stepping in only for safety. Children who are not compared have less need to beat each other.

A grandparent notices the same two defending each other against an outsider on the playground. Rivalry and loyalty live together in siblings, and a bond forged through fights often becomes lifelong support.

A mentor or elder meets a young person's questions with interest, says that honest doubt is old and common, and does not use shame or fear. Being allowed to ask keeps the relationship and often the faith.
Away from home, the young adult skips practices, reads widely and meets people of other faiths and none. The old certainty loosens, bringing both freedom and a sense of loss.
Some feel anger at what they were taught, others a hollow quiet where meaning used to sit. Both are part of the honest process, and rushing to a firm conclusion does not end them.
A young woman notices her partner praising a colleague's talent and feels small. Jealousy is often a comparison in disguise, where she measures herself and finds herself short.
A slow reply, a like on a photo or a night out becomes evidence in her mind. Once suspicious, the brain notices only what confirms the fear and ignores the many ordinary facts against it.

She makes remarks that are half jokes, pulls away to see whether he chases, and sometimes checks his phone. Such tests rarely reassure; they wear both people down and can make the feared outcome real.
He feels distrusted for nothing and starts to keep more private space, which she reads as proof of hiding. The spiral now feeds itself, with each person's protection confirming the other's story.

rows.subtype: Stage 5: Owning the feeling without accusing [Response]
rows.description: She says "I feel insecure when this happens, and I know it is mine to work on. I would like your reassurance, but I will not demand proof." Feelings shared without blame invite care.

She works on her own worth through friends, interests and if needed a counsellor, while he is open and consistent. Trust grows from both, and jealousy that persists despite reassurance is a reason to seek support.
Two children seated together discover they both like cricket cards and start trading. Friendship at this age grows from sharing a bench, a game or a joke, more than from deep knowledge of each other.
The children share a small secret or a snack and watch how the other reacts. Being laughed at would end it; being kept safe invites more, so each small act of trust is quietly checked.
They walk home together, invent codes and say "you are my best friend". There is joy and also possessiveness, with the first hurt when one plays with someone else at recess.
